newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BHP still mulling Australian LNG project.
newsitem.headline: BHP still mulling Australian LNG project.

text.p: The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd said on Wednesday it would make a decision "as soon as possible" about a mooted liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in partnership with Phillips Petroleum Co in Australia's Northern Territory.
"We would hope to be making a decision as soon as possible once it is fully evaluated," a BHP spokesman told Reuters.

International oil major Royal Dutch/Shell Group and local operator Woodside Petroleum Ltd on Wednesday outlined a multi-billion blueprint to commercialise the vast natural gas reserves in Australia's Bonaparte Basin.
The Shell/Woodside project would be located near Darwin, producing 7.5 million tonnes of LNG annually and potentially vying for the same international customers as BHP and Phillips.

Most of the gas from both projects would find its way to the fast-industrialising countries of Asia, who would be required to sign up for deliveries over minimum 20 year periods to ensure commercial viability.
Industry sources familiar with Asia's energy needs said it was unclear whether there would be sufficient market demand for LNG to support both projects in the next five or 10 years
Preliminary blueprints for the projects differ.

The Shell/Woodside plan calls for an initial 18-month study of the construction of two onshore LNG processing plants near Darwin and extensive offshore exploration and infrastructure and transport needs.
Discussions with third parties with offshore gas reserves within the region also are planned.

The BHP/Phillips programme is less advanced, with Phillips favouring a more conventional onshore LNG plant and BHP arguing for an untried offshore facility located at the Bayu Undan gas field in the Timor Sea.
Woodside in equal partnership with five others, including BHP and Shell, already produces 7.5 million tonnes of LNG a year from the North West Shelf, some 2,000 km south of the Bonaparte Basin.
The other partners are the British Petroleum Co Plc, Japan Australia LNG (MiMi) Pty Ltd and Chevron Corp.
Pending firm contracts with buyers from Japanese utility companies, production from the North West Shelf will nearly double early in the next century.
There is also the possibility that the neighbouring undeveloped Gorgon gas field may brought into production.
Earlier this year, Woodside found it had more LNG than it could sell under long-term contracts and was forced to sell it on the international spot market at a discount.
Shell and Woodside estimate their project would generate revenue of between A$35 billion and A$40 billion over 20 years.
Woodside and Shell have said they already have significant gas discoveries in the Sunrise, Troubadour, Loxton Shoals and Evans Shoal gas fields located in the Bonaparte Basin.
They are not yet fully appraised, but are estimated to contain at least five trillion cubic feet of recoverable gas.
The first deliveries of gas from the project would be in around 2005, the companies have said.

Bayu-Undan, which is estimated to contain proven and probable reserves of 3.1 trillion cubic feet of gas and about 400 million barrels of hydrocarbon liquids, will require initial expenditure of more than A$1 billion on facilities to strip condensate and liquefied petroleum gas from reserves, for first production in late 1998.
Total development cost, including an LNG plant, has been estimated at up to A$4.0 billion.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
